terms.Linear regression: Ordinary least squares minimizes ||y - Xw||^2 and has the closed-form solution w = (X^T X)^-1 X^T y, computed in practice with QR or SVD rather than an explicit inverse. Under the Gauss-Markov conditions (linearity, zero-mean errors, constant variance, no correlation between errors) it is the best linear unbiased estimator; with Gaussian noise it is also the maximum-likelihood estimate. Multicollinearity inflates coefficient variance without harming predictions, and outliers with high leverage can dominate the fit, which motivates Huber loss and diagnostics such as Cook's distance. Ridge and lasso add penalties that trade a little bias for lower variance, and generalized linear models extend the idea to counts and binary outcomes.
terms.Logistic regression: Logistic regression maximizes the Bernoulli likelihood, i.e. minimizes log loss, which is convex in the weights, so solvers such as L-BFGS, Newton's method (IRLS) or SAGA reach the global optimum even without a closed form. The gradient is X^T (p - y). Perfectly separable data makes unpenalized weights diverge, which is one reason scikit-learn applies L2 regularization by default (C = 1.0, the inverse penalty strength). The multinomial version uses softmax over classes. Coefficients are odds ratios after exponentiation, and the probability change per unit depends on the baseline (about w/4 near p = 0.5). Probabilities are often reasonably calibrated, but check with a reliability diagram, and tune the decision threshold to error costs.
terms.Decision tree: CART grows binary trees greedily, choosing at each node the feature and threshold that maximize impurity decrease (Gini or entropy for classification, squared or absolute error for regression); finding an optimal tree is NP-hard. Trees are invariant to monotonic feature transforms, model interactions natively and produce axis-aligned decision boundaries, so diagonal relationships need many splits. Without limits they grow until leaves are pure and have very high variance; control depth through max_depth, min_samples_leaf or cost-complexity pruning (ccp_alpha) chosen by cross-validation. Small data perturbations can change the whole structure, which is why trees are mostly used inside ensembles. They cannot extrapolate beyond the range of training targets.
terms.Random forest: For B trees with individual variance sigma^2 and pairwise correlation rho, the ensemble variance is rho sigma^2 + (1 - rho) sigma^2 / B, so adding trees helps only up to the correlation floor and feature subsampling (max_features, often sqrt(d) for classification) lowers rho. Each bootstrap leaves out about 36.8% of rows, giving out-of-bag estimates of error and permutation importance without a separate validation set. Forests are robust defaults that need little tuning and do not overfit as trees are added, but they are memory-heavy, slower to serve with many deep trees, unable to extrapolate, and their impurity-based feature importances are biased toward high-cardinality features. Extremely randomized trees go further by randomizing thresholds too.
terms.Gradient boosting: Gradient boosting performs gradient descent in function space: F_m(x) = F_(m-1)(x) + eta x h_m(x), where h_m is a regression tree fit to the negative gradient of the loss at the current predictions (residuals for squared error). XGBoost uses second-order (Newton) steps and explicit L1/L2 penalties on leaf values; LightGBM uses histogram binning and leaf-wise growth controlled by num_leaves; CatBoost uses symmetric trees and ordered target statistics for categoricals. Key hyperparameters are the learning rate (0.01-0.1), number of trees chosen by early stopping, tree size, minimum samples per leaf and row/column subsampling. Boosting mainly reduces bias and can overfit if run too long, unlike random forests. It handles missing values natively in most libraries.
terms.Support vector machine: The soft-margin SVM minimizes (1/2)||w||^2 + C sum(hinge losses), where hinge loss is max(0, 1 - y f(x)); C is an inverse regularization strength. In the dual, data appears only through dot products, so a positive semi-definite kernel such as RBF, exp(-gamma ||x - x'||^2), yields nonlinear boundaries without computing the feature map. Only points with nonzero dual coefficients, the support vectors, determine the model. C and gamma must be tuned jointly on a log grid, and features must be scaled. Kernel SVM training scales roughly between O(n^2) and O(n^3), so linear SVMs (LinearSVC, SGD with hinge loss) or kernel approximations are used for large data. Outputs are margins, not probabilities, unless calibrated with Platt scaling.
terms.k-nearest neighbors: k-NN is a non-parametric, lazy learner: small k gives low bias and high variance, large k smooths toward the majority class, and k is chosen by cross-validation, often with distance weighting. As data grows, 1-NN's error is at most twice the Bayes error (Cover and Hart). Prediction costs O(n d) by brute force; KD-trees and ball trees help in low dimensions, while approximate nearest-neighbor indexes such as HNSW or IVF-PQ power large-scale vector search over embeddings. In high dimensions distances concentrate and irrelevant features add noise, so scaling, feature selection, dimensionality reduction or learned metrics are essential. Duplicates between training and validation make k-NN look deceptively perfect.
terms.Naive Bayes: Naive Bayes picks argmax over classes of log P(c) + sum log P(x_i | c), computed in log space to avoid underflow. Variants model the likelihood differently: multinomial for word counts, Bernoulli for presence or absence, Gaussian for continuous features, complement NB for imbalanced text. Laplace or Lidstone smoothing (alpha) prevents unseen feature values from zeroing a class. Because correlated features double-count evidence, posterior probabilities are pushed toward 0 and 1 and are poorly calibrated, even when the ranking of classes is right. As a generative model it reaches its asymptotic error with fewer examples than logistic regression, its discriminative counterpart, which is why it shines as a fast baseline on small or sparse datasets.
terms.K-means clustering: Lloyd's algorithm monotonically decreases inertia (within-cluster sum of squared distances) and converges to a local optimum in O(n k d) per iteration; the global problem is NP-hard. k-means++ seeding picks new centroids with probability proportional to squared distance from existing ones, giving an O(log k) approximation in expectation, and multiple restarts (n_init) reduce bad local minima. The method assumes convex, isotropic clusters of similar size, equivalent to a hard-assignment Gaussian mixture with shared spherical covariance. Choose k with silhouette, gap statistic or downstream usefulness rather than the elbow alone. Mini-batch k-means scales to large data; DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, spectral clustering or Gaussian mixtures handle non-spherical or uneven clusters.
terms.Principal component analysis: PCA takes the SVD of centered data X = U S V^T: columns of V are the principal directions (eigenvectors of the covariance matrix) and s_i^2 / (n - 1) are the variances along them (eigenvalues). Projecting onto the top k components gives the best rank-k approximation in squared error (Eckart-Young). Results depend on scaling, so mixed-unit features are usually standardized first, which amounts to PCA on the correlation matrix. PCA is linear, sensitive to outliers and unsupervised, so high-variance directions may not be the predictive ones. Components have arbitrary sign. Variants include randomized, incremental, sparse, kernel and probabilistic PCA, and truncated SVD for sparse text. Fit it on training data only, inside a pipeline.
terms.Lasso regression: Lasso minimizes (1/(2n))||y - Xw||^2 + alpha ||w||_1 in scikit-learn's convention. The L1 ball has corners on the axes, so solutions are sparse; it corresponds to MAP estimation under a Laplace prior. It is solved by coordinate descent with soft-thresholding, and LassoCV traces the full regularization path to choose alpha. Limitations: with d > n it selects at most n features, among correlated features it picks one somewhat arbitrarily, and selected coefficients are biased toward zero. Elastic net (mixing L1 and L2 via l1_ratio) keeps correlated groups together, while relaxed lasso or refitting OLS on the selected features reduces bias. Always standardize features first, since the penalty is unit-dependent.
terms.Feature scaling: StandardScaler maps x to (x - mean) / std, MinMaxScaler to (x - min) / (max - min), RobustScaler uses the median and interquartile range to resist outliers, and MaxAbsScaler preserves sparsity. None of them changes the shape of a distribution; skewed data may need log, Box-Cox or Yeo-Johnson transforms. Scaling improves gradient-descent conditioning, makes L1/L2 penalties treat features fairly and stops large-unit features from dominating distances and PCA. Tree models are invariant to monotonic transforms and need none. The statistics must be learned on training data only and reused at validation, test and serving time; fitting on the full dataset is a classic leakage bug, best prevented by placing the scaler inside a pipeline.
